response.sql: WITH c AS (SELECT o.order_id, COUNT(i.invoice_number) AS n FROM Orders o LEFT JOIN Invoices i ON i.order_id = o.order_id GROUP BY o.order_id), s AS (SELECT order_id, n, n * 1.0 / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Invoices) AS share FROM c), a AS (SELECT AVG(share) AS avg_share FROM s) SELECT SUM(s.n) AS total_invoices, AVG(s.share) AS average_share, AVG(s.share - a.avg_share) AS average_excess_over_average_share FROM s CROSS JOIN a WHERE s.share > a.avg_share

assumptions.assumption: "For each order" covers every row in Orders, so orders with no invoices count as 0 invoices (share 0) and are included in the average share.
The average share is the plain mean of the per-order shares across all orders, and the total is the count of all rows in Invoices.
The 'average share' in the final column is the mean share of the above-average orders. The 'average excess' is measured against the overall average share.

alternatives.interpretation: Only orders that have at least one invoice are considered, so orders with zero invoices are excluded from the average share.
